```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
## 1. Main Question

Do keyboard type (Internal vs. External) and environment
(Quiet vs. Noisy) affect mean Net WPM? Does the effect of
keyboard type depend on the environment?

## 2. Response Variable

The response variable is Net Words Per Minute (Net WPM),
an error-adjusted measure of typing speed. The recorded
values are already Net WPM, so no additional error
deduction is applied in the analysis.

## 3. Experimental Design

This experiment used a 2 × 2 factorial design with two factors:

- Keyboard type: External and Internal.
- Environment: Quiet and Noisy.

Six participants took part: Adnan, Abey, Jason, Sara,
Steven, and Prince. Each participant completed all four
conditions once, producing 24 observations in total.

Each condition was tested by six participants. There
were no repeated trials within the same participant
and condition.

Participant was included as a blocking factor in the
ANOVA to account for differences in baseline typing speed.

## 4. Randomization and Procedure

The order of the four conditions was randomized for
each participant to reduce systematic order effects,
such as practice and fatigue.

Each participant completed one 3-minute typing test
under each keyboard and environment combination.
Net WPM was recorded after each test.

All six participants completed all four conditions.
The dataset contains 24 observations, with no missing
Net WPM values.

## 5. Hypotheses

All tests use a significance level of alpha = 0.05.

### Keyboard Type

H0: Mean Net WPM is equal for Internal and External
keyboards, averaged across environments.

Ha: Mean Net WPM differs between Internal and External
keyboards, averaged across environments.

### Environment

H0: Mean Net WPM is equal for Quiet and Noisy
environments, averaged across keyboard types.

Ha: Mean Net WPM differs between Quiet and Noisy
environments, averaged across keyboard types.

### Interaction

H0: The difference in mean Net WPM between Internal
and External keyboards is the same in both environments.

Ha: The difference in mean Net WPM between Internal
and External keyboards depends on the environment.

## 6. Analysis Method

We calculated mean Net WPM for each keyboard and
environment combination.

We used ANOVA with keyboard type, environment, and
their interaction. Participant was included as a
blocking factor to account for baseline differences
in typing speed.

The fitted model was:

Net WPM ~ Participant + Keyboard + Environment
+ Keyboard:Environment

F-tests were used to test the three hypotheses at
alpha = 0.05. An interaction plot was used to compare
the keyboard differences across environments.

Residual plots and a Shapiro-Wilk test were used
to assess model assumptions. The model assumes
additive participant effects and independent errors
with constant variance and an approximately normal
distribution.


```{r}
typing <- read.csv(
  "/Users/suchiajung/Desktop/Typing_speed.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(typing)[5] <- "Net_WPM"

typing$Participant <- factor(trimws(typing$Participant))
typing$Keyboard <- factor(
  trimws(typing$Keyboard),
  levels = c("External", "Internal")
)
typing$Environment <- factor(
  trimws(typing$Environment),
  levels = c("Quiet", "Noisy")
)

typing <- typing[
  c("Participant", "Trial", "Keyboard", "Environment", "Net_WPM")
]

typing
```

```{r}

nrow(typing)
nlevels(typing$Participant)

colSums(is.na(typing))

with(typing, table(Participant, Keyboard, Environment))
```

```{r}
aggregate(
  Net_WPM ~ Keyboard + Environment,
  data = typing,
  FUN = mean
)

aggregate(
  Net_WPM ~ Keyboard,
  data = typing,
  FUN = mean
)

aggregate(
  Net_WPM ~ Environment,
  data = typing,
  FUN = mean
)
```

```{r}
model <- aov(
  Net_WPM ~ Participant + Keyboard * Environment,
  data = typing
)

summary(model)
```
## 7. ANOVA Results

After accounting for participant differences, keyboard
type was significant, F(1, 15) = 13.307, p = 0.00238.
We reject the null hypothesis for keyboard type.

Mean Net WPM was 42.67 for Internal keyboards and
37.83 for External keyboards, a difference of
approximately 4.83 Net WPM.

Environment was not significant,
F(1, 15) = 0.016, p = 0.90157.
We fail to reject the null hypothesis for environment.

The keyboard-by-environment interaction was not
significant, F(1, 15) = 0.016, p = 0.90157.
We fail to reject the null hypothesis for interaction.

These results provide evidence of a keyboard difference
under the fitted model, but insufficient evidence of
an environment effect or an interaction.
```{r}
with(typing, interaction.plot(
  x.factor = Keyboard,
  trace.factor = factor(
    Environment,
    levels = c("Noisy", "Quiet")
  ),
  response = Net_WPM,
  fun = mean,
  type = "b",
  pch = c(16, 16),
  col = c("red", "blue"),
  lty = c(1, 1),
  xlab = "Keyboard Type",
  ylab = "Mean Net WPM",
  trace.label = "Environment",
  main = "Interaction Plot: Keyboard × Environment"
))
```
## 8. Interaction Plot Interpretation

Mean Net WPM increased from External to Internal
keyboards in both environments.

In the Quiet environment, the mean increased from
38.00 to 42.67 Net WPM. In the Noisy environment,
it increased from 37.67 to 42.67 Net WPM.

The two lines are nearly parallel, suggesting similar
keyboard differences across environments. This agrees
with the nonsignificant interaction test (p = 0.90157).

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(model, which = 1)
plot(model, which = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

shapiro.test(residuals(model))
```

## 9. Model Diagnostics

The residuals-versus-fitted plot showed a slight curve
but no clear funnel pattern. The Q-Q plot showed points
approximately following the reference line, with some
deviations in the tails.

The Shapiro-Wilk test gave W = 0.96589 and p = 0.5674.
At alpha = 0.05, we found insufficient evidence that
the residuals depart from a normal distribution.

These checks did not reveal strong evidence of severe
non-normality or unequal variance. However, the small
sample limits the ability to detect assumption violations.
These plots do not establish independence of errors.

## 10. Limitations and Future Improvements

The experiment included only six participants, with
one trial per participant in each condition. This
limits generalization and our ability to detect
small environment or interaction effects.

The 24 observations came from repeated measurements
of six people, rather than 24 independent participants.
Our model accounts for baseline participant differences
but assumes that participant effects are additive.

Keyboard familiarity may have influenced performance,
but it was not measured in this dataset.

If we repeated the experiment, we would recruit more
participants, repeat each condition within participants,
and record keyboard familiarity and actual test order.
We would also standardize passage difficulty, noise
level, and rest periods.

## 11. Conclusion

Under the fitted participant-blocked ANOVA model,
keyboard type was associated with a significant
difference in mean Net WPM.

Internal keyboards averaged 42.67 Net WPM, compared
with 37.83 for External keyboards, a difference of
approximately 4.83 Net WPM.

We found insufficient evidence of an environment
effect or a keyboard-by-environment interaction.
The conclusions are limited to the participants
and conditions studied.
